analysis.one_liner: Speeds approval of cheaper biosimilar copies of brand-name biologic drugs by easing trial requirements.
analysis.headline: The Senate HELP Committee reported the bill favorably with a bipartisan substitute amendment in July 2026 and placed it on the Senate calendar, where it awaits a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Biologic drugs — made from living cells, often treating cancer and autoimmune disease — are among the most expensive medicines, and cheaper copycat versions called biosimilars must pass FDA review before they can compete. Current law makes applicants run clinical efficacy studies to prove their biosimilar works like the brand-name original. This bill removes that default requirement and lets the FDA demand an efficacy study only when it gives written notice explaining why it is necessary, and it also ends the rule that the same FDA office that reviewed the original brand drug must review the biosimilar. The stated goal is to get lower-priced biosimilars to patients faster.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who take expensive biologic drugs, if faster approvals bring more biosimilar competition and lower prices; and the companies that develop biosimilars, who face a shorter, cheaper path to market.

how_it_helps.text: The bill eliminates the default requirement that a biosimilar applicant submit a clinical efficacy study, leaving the FDA free to require one only when it deems it necessary [S2].
If the FDA does require an efficacy study, it must give the applicant a written justification, with a 60-day deadline after application submission to make that determination [S2].
The bill also removes the requirement that a biosimilar application be reviewed by the same FDA division that reviewed the reference brand-name product, shortening the review path [S2].
Cheaper biosimilar competition is aimed at biologic drugs, a category that includes many of the highest-priced medicines in the United States [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name biologic makers face faster competition on their flagship products, and patients bear a small residual safety risk if streamlined reviews catch fewer differences between the copy and the original.

drawbacks.text: The bill constrains FDA discretion: once the agency makes a written determination about what studies are needed, it cannot amend it to require an efficacy study later except by written agreement with the sponsor or with a detailed written scientific justification [S3].

Reducing required clinical testing could mean fewer opportunities to detect clinically meaningful differences between a biosimilar and the brand-name original, a trade-off supporters accept to speed access and cut prices; the reported version does keep the requirement for an immunogenicity assessment [S2].
The bill does nothing directly to lower the price of existing brand-name biologics; any savings depend on biosimilar makers actually entering the market and competing on price.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real and modest: skipping routine efficacy trials for drugs that are near-copies of already-approved medicines saves years and tens of millions of dollars per applicant, which should mean more biosimilars and more price competition in a market where biologics dominate the top of the drug-cost ladder. The safety cost appears limited — the reported version still requires pharmacokinetic and immunogenicity data — but the bill does handcuff the FDA's ability to demand additional efficacy data late in the process, and that restriction serves applicants, not patients.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared the Senate Health Committee on a favorable bipartisan report in July 2026 and now sits on the Senate legislative calendar waiting for floor time; it has not come to a vote and the House has not acted on it.

narrative.text: Rand Paul introduced the bill in April 2025, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee [S1].
Two senators cosponsored it — one Republican and one Democrat, Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire [S4].
On July 22, 2026, the HELP Committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, and on July 27 it was reported by Senator Cassidy [S5].

The committee substitute rewrote the bill: it keeps a required assessment of pharmacokinetics and immunogenicity, allows the FDA to require pharmacodynamics or efficacy studies only with a written determination of necessity, and strikes the same-division review requirement [S3].
On July 27, 2026, the bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 520 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, biosimilar developers gained ground — a shorter, cheaper approval path cleared committee — while brand-name biologic makers keep their current pricing power until the bill actually becomes law.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican senator sponsored the bill with a Democratic cosponsor, and the Republican committee chair reported it favorably; no opposition appears anywhere in the action record [S4].

industries.note: Faster biosimilar approvals bring copycat competition to their most profitable products sooner, pressuring the prices of drugs that anchor their revenue. Every year of delay in biosimilar entry is a year of monopoly pricing they keep.

Dropping the default efficacy-study requirement cuts years and major costs off each approval, so more of these companies can enter the market. Their gain arrives as cheaper alternatives for patients, so their interest and the public's run together here.

The bill gives the agency flexibility to skip efficacy studies it deems unnecessary, but it also strips the requirement that the same division that reviewed the original drug review the biosimilar and restricts the agency from amending its study determinations later without written justification. The agency gains efficiency but loses case-by-case control.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has bipartisan sponsorship and cleared committee favorably, but it sits on the Senate calendar with no scheduled floor time and no House counterpart action. Small bipartisan health bills at this stage often wait months for floor time and frequently move only when attached to a larger package such as an FDA user-fee reauthorization; a standalone vote is possible but not the default.
